title: Rivers in the Sky Are Soaking the Pacific Northwest
summary:
The Pacific Northwest is getting soaked this week. Heavy rain and the year's highest tides, called king tides, are hitting the West Coast. Two more atmospheric rivers will soak Oregon and Washington on Friday and Saturday, after two others dropped inches of rain.

What is an atmospheric river? Think of it as a river in the sky: a narrow band of water vapor that wind pushes along. It drops rain or snow widely, and can stretch 2,000 miles long and 600 miles wide, said F. Martin Ralph, a researcher at Scripps.

These rivers are natural, and about 50 to 60 percent of California's rain comes from them, said Josh Weiss, a meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The season runs from October to March, and this year started fast.

Trouble comes when several arrive in a row, bringing flash floods and landslides, Weiss said. Washington's coast could see 20-foot waves this weekend, said Jeff Michalski of the National Weather Service in Seattle. FEMA data show these rivers cause 90 percent or more of flood damage in the Western U.S.
why_it_matters: It matters because heavy rain, floods, and huge waves can make roads unsafe, close schools, and keep kids from playing safely outside.

background_read: An atmospheric river is like a river in the sky: a long, narrow band of water vapor that wind carries across the ocean and over land.
When it reaches land, it drops its water as rain or snow, which can soak a wide area.
These rivers are a natural part of how rain reaches the West Coast, but when several arrive one after another, the heavy rain can cause floods and landslides.

WHAT: Heavy rain and the year's highest tides, called king tides, are hitting the West Coast, with two more atmospheric rivers arriving on Friday and Saturday after two others dropped inches of rain
WHERE: The Pacific Northwest, especially Oregon and Washington and the West Coast
WHY: Several atmospheric rivers are arriving in a row, and these natural bands of water vapor can drop rain or snow widely over a large area
